author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Field Test for Trust
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The first argument between Severus Snape and Paladin Danse began over a glass of water.

It was a sample jar, technically, with a label I had written in blue ink and a number beneath it. The jar had been filled from the repaired Brasswatch purifier. Danse wanted to know whether it was safe to return the machine to service. Severus wanted to know why someone had thought a clear liquid proved anything.

"Visual inspection is the first stage," Danse said.

"Then it is fortunate you have reached the stage at which looking becomes insufficient."

Danse folded his arms.

I stood between them with a clipboard, wondering whether I should have brought a referee.

It was supposed to be an ordinary afternoon. A new gasket had arrived from the local supplier, the workshop floor had been braced, and the purifier had run through two pressure tests without leaking. Fen wanted the water quality independently checked before neighbors carried it home. Danse had agreed to call in a second specialist.

He had not expected that specialist to wear black robes and treat every statement as something he might be able to correct.

"Professor," Danse said, "we've already completed the mechanical inspection."

"Excellent. Then I trust you will have no objection to examining what the water contains."

"I brought samples."

"Unsealed samples."

"They're labeled."

"An impressive defense against airborne contaminants."

I made a note that looked like words but was mostly a plea for patience.

Severus looked at my clipboard.

"Are you recording this?"

"Every useful thing."

"Then you have very little writing to do."

Danse's jaw tightened. There were moments when he still carried rank inside his shoulders, even without the armor. He had learned to take off the insignia. That did not make it easy to hear a civilian dismiss a test he'd spent two days conducting.

I set the jar on the table.

"Can we agree on what we're trying to establish?"

Severus answered first.

"Whether the water is potable."

"Whether the entire system is reliable," Danse corrected.

"Good," I said. "Two different questions. We need both answered."

For a moment neither man spoke.

Then Danse nodded once.

"Agreed."

Severus inclined his head with microscopic politeness.

That was as much peace as I expected.

We conducted the first checks at Moonroot Archive. Severus prepared reagent strips and a simple analysis that would detect common chemical contaminants. Danse carried a mechanical pressure gauge, temperature probe, and enough spare seals to start another purifier if necessary.

Tamsin arrived with a repair ledger. She had agreed to record the results because she did not have a romantic interest in either specialist being right.

"Do you have a romantic interest in the water?" I asked.

"Only if it stops leaking on my floor."

Pip delivered the next sample jar, sealed with a numbered strip. A neighbor named Edda brought a control sample from the safe hand pump. Neri checked that the jars had been collected at different times of day.

For the first hour, everything looked good.

The water tested clean. The pressure stayed stable. The new gasket held.

Danse made a small, satisfied mark in his ledger.

Severus did not appear satisfied.

"Again," he said.

"We've already tested it at operating pressure."

"Then perhaps it will survive the unbearable ordeal of being tested once more."

"You're not familiar with this machinery."

"And you are not familiar with the reagents."

Tamsin put down her pencil.

"I'm familiar with the fact that the people in the square need water," she said. "Either show me a reason the second test matters or stop using my workroom for a contest."

That quieted them.

Severus considered the sample.

"The chemical content may change after the pump has been idle," he said. "Some residues appear only after water has remained in contact with the fittings."

Danse's posture changed.

"That is a valid concern."

"Yes," Severus said. "It is."

"Then we test after an idle period."

"Exactly."

I nearly applauded.

Instead I asked Tamsin to write down the plan, because a plan that existed only in the heads of two stubborn men was not a plan I trusted.

We left the purifier switched off for the required period and went to the square for lunch. Iroh had set out bread, pickles, and a pot of soup. Greg was adjusting a bench near Starwake Pier, humming something too quiet to hear properly.

Danse ate as if he were still on duty. Severus ate as if the soup had personally inconvenienced him.

Iroh sat with us and poured tea.

"You are both very serious about water," he observed.

"It's essential," Danse said.

"It is," Iroh agreed. "Especially for making tea."

Severus stared into his cup.

"I suspect you have arranged this remark in advance."

"Only by several decades."

I laughed. Danse looked uncertain whether laughter was permitted during a technical discussion.

"Eat your bread," I told him.

"I am."

"More enthusiastically."

"That isn't a measurable standard."

"Severus, please tell him he's being difficult."

"He is being precise. A rare comfort."

Iroh smiled over his cup.

By late afternoon, we returned to Brasswatch. Pip opened the valve while Danse watched the gauge. The needle rose to the expected mark. The fittings stayed dry.

Severus took a sample and applied his reagent.

Nothing happened.

Then, on the third jar, the strip at the edge of the table shifted color.

It was subtle, a pale change that could have been dismissed as a flaw in the paper.

Severus held it to the lamp.

Danse leaned close.

"That is not present in the control."

"No."

"Corrosion?"

"Possibly."

They both looked toward the purifier.

I checked the collection log. The third jar had been filled after the machine had sat overnight. Its temperature was lower than the others. The number was written clearly beside the sample.

"Could it be coming from the old intake pipe rather than the replacement fitting?" I asked.

Danse examined the diagram.

Severus compared the reagent results.

They answered at nearly the same time.

"Yes."

I tried not to look smug.

"Then the gasket was never the only issue," I said.

"No," Danse admitted.

Severus set the strip down.

"The discovery does not invalidate your repair."

"It does invalidate the assumption that the system is ready."

"Yes."

Danse nodded, accepting the uncomfortable fact without trying to save face.

We shut the purifier down again. It was disappointing. The temporary water station would have to remain open another week, and the neighbors would need a new schedule for carrying water.

But nobody had been sent home with a false promise.

After the others left, Severus remained beside the bench while I finished the report.

"You enjoyed that," he said.

"The part where people listened to each other?"

"The part where I was made to concede the value of a mechanical inspection."

"That was delightful, yes."

He looked down at the sample jar.

"It would have been easy to claim my test had found the problem and his had not."

"Why didn't you?"

"Because that would be inaccurate."

I studied him.

He saw the affection on my face and narrowed his eyes.

"Do not make a spectacle of it."

"Wouldn't dream of it."

Danse returned at the doorway carrying the old pipe section.

"Professor Snape. I wanted to thank you for the second test."

Severus inclined his head.

"And I wish to see the pressure data before we attempt another chemical analysis."

Danse's mouth twitched.

"I've made copies."

"Then perhaps you are not entirely hopeless."

He left before the insult could become a compliment.

I leaned against Severus's shoulder.

"You two are going to be friends."

"That is a baseless accusation."

"Would you prefer colleagues?"

"I would prefer not to be psychoanalyzed over a water filter."

"Then come home."

He looked toward the lanterns glowing in the yard.

"In a moment."

We stood for a little while longer, watching the temporary pump being used safely by people who knew precisely what it could and could not do. The water from the repaired machine would need another test. The report would need another page.

Severus took my hand when I offered it.

For once, neither of us confused an unfinished answer with failure.
